cards.explanation: The answer is forty. The text says Joash "…reigned in Jerusalem forty years." Joash is the king of Judah here, and forty years is a long run on any job. I've had oven mitts that didn't last half that.

The answer is True. The text says Joash "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest." Jehoiada is the priest who has been guiding him. A good teacher at your elbow is like a timer next to the oven: things come out better.
The word is removed. The text says, "Nevertheless, the high places were not removed…" Joash did right, yet those places were still there. The people kept sacrificing and burning incense at them.

The answer is all the money brought as sacred gifts. Joash tells the priests, "Collect all the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD…" He names the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. So this is money brought as sacred gifts for the house of the LORD.

The answer is repairing damage in the temple. Joash says, "…let it be used to repair any damage found in the temple." The money gets ONE job, friends, and it doesn't wander off. Most of us can't say that about our paychecks. Mine shows up, takes one look at the bills, and vanishes by Tuesday.

The answer is False. The text says that by the twenty-third year, the priests had not yet repaired the damage to the temple. That's a lot of years for one to-do item. I've seen dishes sit in the sink that long, and I'm not proud of it.

The answer is that Joash asks why they haven't repaired the temple. He says, "Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?" By the twenty-third year of his reign the damage still hadn't been repaired (2 Kings 12:6). So he calls in Jehoiada and the other priests to ask. I'd want a very good answer ready for that one.

The order is to take no more and hand it over. Joash says, "Now, therefore, take no more money from your constituency, but hand it over for the repair of the temple." The order has two parts. The priests are to take no more, and they are to hand it over for the repair of the temple.

The answer is False. The priests agreed not to receive money from the people, and also "…that they would not repair the temple themselves." The job moves to someone else. I bet they were relieved to put that one down.

The answer is beside the altar. Jehoiada set the chest "…beside the altar on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD." Jehoiada is the priest who took the chest and bored a hole in its lid. That puts it right where people come in.

The answer is the royal scribe and the high priest. When they saw a large amount of money in the chest, "…the royal scribe and the high priest would go up, count the money…" Then they tied it up in bags. The king's scribe and the high priest on one chest? I'd trust that pair with my cookie jar.

The answer is the carpenters and stonecutters. The supervisors paid those doing the work: "the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters." That's the crew actually fixing the house of the LORD. The money went to the people with the tools.

The answer is True. The text says they "…purchased timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to the house of the LORD…" They also paid the other expenses of the repairs. All of it was aimed at the repair work.

The answer is False. The text says the money "…was not used for making silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any articles of gold or silver…" It went to the workers who repaired the house of the LORD. Shiny extras had to wait.

The answer is because they acted with integrity. The text says no accounting was required from the men who received the money, "…because they acted with integrity." That's the reason the text gives. Honest people can handle money without anybody hovering over them.

The word is priests. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings "…was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests." So that money was not part of what came into the house of the LORD. The verse names the priests, so that's the word that fits the blank.

The answer is that Joash sends Hazael the sacred objects. Joash "…took all the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers…" and sent them to Hazael. Hazael is the king of Aram, who had captured Gath and decided to attack Jerusalem. The text says that after Joash sent them, Hazael withdrew.

The word is gold. Joash sent Hazael "…all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace…" He also sent the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah, plus his own consecrated items. That was a big load to send.

The answer is True. The text says, "So Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem." Hazael, king of Aram, had decided to attack, but he pulled back after Joash sent the gifts. Joash had sent him the sacred objects and gold before that.

The answer is his own servants. The text says, "…the servants of Joash rose up and formed a conspiracy and killed him…" This is a heavy part of the story. It happened at Beth-millo, on the road down to Silla.

The answer is with his fathers in the City of David. The text says, "…they buried him with his fathers in the City of David…" Joash was laid to rest among the kings before him. His story closes quietly.
The name is Amaziah. The text says, "…his son Amaziah reigned in his place." The crown stays in the family. The story of Judah's kings keeps rolling.
